sagebrush control to realize improved range condition and forage
productivity towards reaching site potential.

Actual_Implementation: Two pounds of a low volatile ester of 2,4-D mixed with 4 2/3 gallons of water were applied per acre by two small Pawnee aircraft[s]. The operation was carried out by a commercial applicator under the direction of the Bureau of Land Management.\r\n\r\nTreatment applied in alternating strip pattern.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Pesticide surveillance activities were undertaken in order to gain some information
as to the effects of the chemical itself on resident fish, bird, and
mammal populations. Visual observations were made before, during, and after
the spray application and any effects noted. Pre-spray and 15 day post-spray
samples of vegetation (sagebrush, grasses, grouse food plants, etc.), resident
birds (horned larks, blackbirds, waterfowl) and mammals (ground squirrels) were
collected for 2,4-D residue analyses.
The only waters within the spray area were several livestock watering ponds
(2-5 acres) which contained no fish but were used fairly extensively for waterfowl
nesting. However, all of the sprayed area drained into the North Platte
River, an excellent trout stream. It would be expected that some 2,4-D may
enter the North Platte River through runoff from the treated area following
periods of rainfall. Thus, samples of brown trout and suckers were collected
from the North Platte downstream from the spray area for 2,4-D residue analyses.
These collections were made about 90 days after the spray material had been
applied. At the same time a few additional samples of waterfowl and other
birds were collected from the sprayed area.

to some extent and the definite pattern of alternate sprayed and unsprayed
strips could be readily observed. Some of the broadleaved plants in the understory
were curled and turning brown.
Visual observations indicated little or no direct effect of the spray operation
on resident birds and mammals . Birds, including horned larks, blackbirds and
waterfowl, and mammals, including ground squirrels and antelope, appeared to be
equally as abundant and active during, and up to three months after, the spray
application as had been observed previously.
No fish were present in the only waters, a few small stock ponds, within the
spray area and thus no observations could be made as to the effects of a direct
application on fish. However, the treated area drained into the North Platte
River, but was only a small portion of the total North Platte drainage.
Observations and collections in the North Platte below the treated area indicated
no effects on bottom animal or trout populations.
Residue analyses for 2,4-D showed considerable buildup in plant tissues following
the spray application. However, the levels reached (maximum 14 ppm) were far
below those which were known to produce physiological damage when fed to waterfowl.
Analyses of animal tissues also showed small residues of 2,4-D, although
the results were quite variable and no definite conclusions could be drawn from
these data.
Residue levels in some fish samples from the North Platte River were surprisingly
high considering the fact that no 2,4-D was applied directly, and the area
sprayed was only a small part of the total North Platte drainage.

Wildlife biologists from the Colorado Game, Fish and Parks Department and the
Colorado Cooperative Wildlife Research Unit are continuing studies of the effect
of the different spray patterns on the sage grouse population. However, it will
probably be several years before any definite conclusions can be drawn from
these studies .
Recommendations
If extensive sagebrush control operations continue in the North Park area,
additional observations and studies should be made with respect to effects on
fish and wildlife. On the basis of observations and available information,
2,4-D at the normal rate used for sagebrush control would not be expected to have
a directly toxic effect on fish or wildlife. However, little information is
available on long range effects, either from the standpoint of the accumulation
of chemical residues in tissues or from changes in environmental conditions.
Such studies would be somewhat beyond the scope of normal pesticide surveillance
activities.
Studies of the long range effects of different patterns of spraying on the sage
grouse population, mainly from the standpoint of habitat alteration, are
presently being conducted by the Colorado Game, Fish and Parks Department and
the Colorado Cooperative Wildlife Research Unit. Such studies should be expanded
to include 2,4-D residue information and possible physiological effects of the
chemical on wildlife species.

Studies of long range effects of chemical sagebrush control on the sport fishery
could be carried out by Cooperative Fishery Units or other research groups.
Information should be obtained on 2,4-D residue levels in fish and fish food
organisms as well as possible effects of the chemical on basic productivity and
fish reproduction. Information on possible side effects such as tainting of
fish flesh, oxygen depletion in ponds from decaying vegetation, and effects of
streambank vegetation removal on the environment could also be obtained. North
Park with its variety of excellent fishing waters might be a suitable site for
such studies.

Actual_Implementation: Two pounds of a low volatile ester of 2,4-D mixed with 4 2/3 gallons of water were applied per acre by two small Pawnee aircraft[s]. The operation was carried out by a commercial applicator under the direction of the Bureau of Land Management.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
The first observations were made during the period immediately preceding the
spray operation and for several days during the actual spraying. Although an
effort was made to find them, no sage grouse or grouse nests were observed.
The major land birds in the area were horned larks, field sparrows and blackbirds.
Several hundred waterfowl were using the stock ponds. Teal were nesting in the
sagebrush away from the water and several nests containing five or six eggs
were found. At least 20 avocets were using one pond and three nests containing
four eggs each were found on the barren ground near the waters edge. Ground
squirrels were the only small mammals observed in abundance in the area, although
one badger was seen. A small herd of antelope was using the area and was seen
on several occasions .
Observations during the actual spraying indicated little or no change from
pre-spray conditions . Resident birds and mammals appeared to be just as abundant
and active as before. Waterfowl remained on the ponds and did not appear to be
disturbed. At least some of the antelope remained in the area and did not even
pay much attention to the spray planes.
Observations two weeks after the spray application showed practically no changes
from those previously. No noticeable change in numbers or activity of birds or
mammals was noted . Some broadleaved plants had begun to curl and turn brown
but there was little noticeable effect on the sagebrush.
Additional observations were made on September 4 and 5, about three months
after the spray application. The sprayed strips of sagebrush had begun to
discolor and a definite demarcation between sprayed and unsprayed strips could
be noted (Figure 12). Waterfowl were more abundant on ponds in the sprayed
area than had been noted at any time previously. Numerous field sparrows and
horned larks were also observed. Several antelope were still using the area .
No ground squirrels were seen at this time but probably because of weather
conditions.
At the time these latter observations were made, a look was also taken at the
North Platte River downstream from the spray area, Samples taken in riffle
areas with a hand screen showed a good population of bottom animals, including
mayfly, stonefly, and caddisfly larvae. An overnight set with a gill net
collected six large (14"-17") brown trout and about two dozen suckers (8"-16"),
which were retained for 2,4-D residue analyses.
Field Studies and Results
Other than visual observations the only field studies conducted were the
determination of water quality characteristics of several waters and the
collection of pre-spray and post-spray samples of vegetation, birds, mammals,
and fish for 2,4-D residue analyses .
Water analyses were conducted with a field chemical kit on September 4 [report shows results].
The livestock pond was highly alkaline and probably would not support fish even
if stocked or access to fish were available. Conditions in the North Platte
River would appear quite satisfactory for a productive fishery.
Samples of land vegetation, including sagebrush, rabbitbrush, grasses, and
major broadleaved plants were collected for residue analyses, pre-spray and
two-weeks post-spray. Approximately 200 grams live weight were cut or picked
from random areas, put in plastic bags and kept in an ice chest until returned
to the laboratory freezer.
Birds and mammals were collected with a 410 gauge shotgun, placed whole in
plastic bags and iced until returned to the freezer.
The frozen samples were delivered to Spectran Laboratories in Denver for 2,4-D
residue analyses, In the laboratory, feet, head, and feathers were removed
from birds and feet, head and fur from mammals. The samples were then either
processed whole or divided into two parts, structure and viscera. Fish were
either processed whole or divided into structure and viscera.
Collection dates, the types of samples, and the results of 2,4-D analyses as
reported by Spectran Laboratories, Inc. are shown in Tables 1 and 2.
Discussion
There was no indication that the applications of 2,4-D had any immediate
harmful effects on fish, bird or mammal populations. Any long range effects,
either from the chemical or from environmental changes will necessarily have
to await the results of additional studies.
The results of residue analyses indicate that 2,4-D does concentrate to some
extent in vegetation and animal tissues. However , results on similar samples
were quite variable with no definite trends shown. The few samples of birds
collected 90 days after the spray application showed lower residues than those
collected 15 days after, which might indicate some loss in residues during this
period. However, it is not known whether these birds were continuous residents
of the area or were recent migrants.
It was surprising that no 2,4-D residues were found in post spray samples of
aquatic vegetation and bottom muds from a pond within the spray area. Heavy
rains had previously occurred and it was expected that some 2,4-D would be
washed into the pond.
The 2,4-D residues in some of the North Platte fish were surprisingly high,
considering that the sprayed area was such a small part of the total drainage .
Unfortunately no pre-spray fish samples were taken and the 2,4-D residue can
not definitely be attributed to this particular operation. Other areas in the
North Platte drainage have been treated in previous years. If possible, in
the future some additional fish-residue data should be obtained from waters
treated directly with 2,4-D or at least from those where the treated area is
a much larger portion of the total drainage.
